title: Intestinal microbial metabolism of phosphatidylcholine and cardiovascular risk
authors: Tang WH, Wang Z, Levison BS, Koeth RA, Britt EB, Fu X, et al.
population: Challenge study: 40 healthy adults given two hard-boiled eggs (about 250 mg total choline each) and 250 mg d9-phosphatidylcholine; 6 of them repeated the challenge after 1 week of metronidazole 500 mg twice daily and ciprofloxacin 500 mg once daily, and again at least 1 month after withdrawal. Outcome study: 4007 adults undergoing elective diagnostic cardiac catheterisation at the Cleveland Clinic (GeneBank), mean age 63 years, 64% men.

result: After the challenge, plasma TMAO and d9-TMAO rose over time; in the 6 participants given antibiotics, TMAO and d9-TMAO in plasma and urine were almost completely suppressed, and both were again readily detectable at least 1 month after withdrawal. In the outcome study, 513 of 4007 participants had a major adverse cardiovascular event (death from any cause, non-fatal myocardial infarction or non-fatal stroke) within 3 years. Highest (above 6.18 µM) against lowest (below 2.43 µM) TMAO quartile: unadjusted hazard ratio 2.54 (95% CI 1.96 to 3.28); adjusted for traditional risk factors and hs-CRP 1.88 (1.44 to 2.44); further adjusted for myeloperoxidase, eGFR, white-cell count, body-mass index and medications 1.49 (1.10 to 2.03); further adjusted for angiographic extent of coronary disease 1.43 (1.05 to 1.94). Per 1 SD of TMAO: unadjusted 1.40 (1.29 to 1.51), adjusted 1.30 (1.20 to 1.41). Event counts by quartile are not given in the text. Intestinal microbiota convert the choline moiety of dietary phosphatidylcholine into trimethylamine, which hepatic flavin-containing monooxygenases convert into TMAO, which is excreted in urine.
